summary: Describes using Hierarchical Host Identity Tags as self-asserting IPv6 addresses to serve as trustable identifiers for drones in Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID. In this role they are called DRIP Entity Tags. It updates RFC 7401 and another related RFC.

plainLanguage.summary: A drone broadcasts its ID so people on the ground can tell what it is. This RFC builds that ID from the drone's own cryptographic key, so the drone can prove the ID belongs to it, and adds a small piece of routing information that points to the registry where the ID is listed.

subtitle: Self-asserting IPv6 addresses that give every drone a hard-to-fake ID and a pointer to its registry.

tldr.problem: Drone Remote ID needs an identifier that is unique, hard to spoof, tells observers which registry lists it, and fits in 19 characters.
tldr.mechanism: Hierarchical Host Identity Tags put a 28-bit registry hierarchy and an 8-bit suite ID next to a 64-bit hash of the drone's public key, forming a 128-bit IPv6 address. When used for drones they are called DRIP Entity Tags.
tldr.outcome: A DET is only trustable together with registration and proof of key ownership. The RFC says plainly that the 64-bit hash is small enough that registration is a MUST.

today: RFC 9374 is a Proposed Standard, published in March 2023. It updates RFC 7343 and RFC 7401. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it.

sections.title: A Trustable Identifier for Drones
sections.content:
The Drone Remote ID Protocol requirements (RFC 9153) describe an Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID as unique, non-spoofable, and identifying a registry where the ID is listed, all within a 19-character identifier. This RFC is a foundational document of DRIP: it describes the use of Hierarchical Host Identity Tags (HHITs) as self-asserting IPv6 addresses, and thereby a trustable identifier for use as the UAS Remote ID. All other DRIP-related technologies will enable or use HHITs as multipurpose remote identifiers.

HHITs add explicit hierarchy to the 128-bit Host Identity Tag space, enabling DNS HHIT queries and use with a differentiated access control such as the Registration Data Access Protocol (RFC 9224) for third-party identification endorsement. The addition of hierarchy to HITs is an extension to RFC 7401 and requires an update to RFC 7343. As the document also adds EdDSA for Host Identities, a number of HIP parameters in RFC 7401 are updated, but these should not be needed in a DRIP implementation that does not use HIP.

HHITs used within the context of UAS are labelled DRIP Entity Tags. The RFC uses HHIT when covering the technology and DET in the context of UAS RID. HHITs provide self-claims of the HHIT registry, and a HHIT can only be in a single registry within a registry system such as DNS. HHITs are valid, though non-routable, IPv6 addresses, so they fit in many ways within various IETF technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a serial number that anyone can print on a label, the drone's ID is derived from the cryptographic key inside it. The drone signs with that key, and the ID shows which authority issued it and which registry lists it.

sections.title: The Layout of a HHIT
sections.content:
The HHIT is a small but important enhancement over the flat Host Identity Tag space, constructed as an Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash IDentifier (ORCHID) (RFC 7343). By adding two levels of hierarchical administration control, the HHIT provides for device registration and ownership, enhancing the trust framework for HITs.

The 128-bit HHITs represent the host identity in only a 64-bit hash, rather than the 96 bits in HITs. Four of the 32 freed-up bits expand the Suite ID to 8 bits, and the other 28 bits are used to create a hierarchical administration organization for HIT domains. A HHIT is built from the following fields: an IPv6 prefix of at most 28 bits; a 28-bit Hierarchy ID, which is divided into a 14-bit Registered Assigning Authority and a 14-bit HHIT Domain Authority; an 8-bit HHIT Suite ID; and the ORCHID hash, which is 92 minus the prefix length, for example 64 bits.

The IPv6 HHIT prefix MUST be distinct from the one used in the flat-space HIT as allocated in RFC 7343, because without a distinct prefix the first four bits of the RAA would be interpreted as the HIT Suite ID under HIPv2. The prefix 2001:30::/28 is assigned for DET use and registered in the IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry. Other prefixes may be added later, either for DET use or other applications of HHITs; for a prefix to be added to the registry, its usage and HID allocation process have to be publicly available.

The HHIT Suite IDs specify the host identity and hash algorithms, and are a superset of the 4-bit and 8-bit HIT Suite IDs defined in RFC 7401. HHIT values 1 to 15 map to the basic 4-bit HIT Suite IDs, values 17 to 31 to the extended 8-bit ones, and values unique to HHIT start at 32. Because HHIT introduces a new Suite ID, EdDSA with cSHAKE128, and because this is of value to HIPv2, it is allocated out of the 4-bit HIT space. The defined suite IDs are RSA with DSA or SHA-256 as 1, ECDSA with SHA-384 as 2, ECDSA_LOW with SHA-1 as 3, and EdDSA with cSHAKE128 as 5. Two further values, 254 and 255, are reserved for domain authority private use, which may be used for large-scale experimentation with post-quantum computing hashes or similar domain-specific needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is laid out in pieces: a reserved prefix saying what the address is for, a 28-bit registry pointer, an 8-bit code saying which cryptographic algorithms were used, and a 64-bit hash of the drone's public key.

sections.title: The Two Levels of the Hierarchy
sections.content:
The Hierarchy ID provides the structure to organize HITs into administrative domains. It is divided into a 14-bit Registered Assigning Authority and a 14-bit HHIT Domain Authority. The rationale for splitting the HID into two 14-bit domains is described in Appendix B of the RFC.

An RAA is a business or organization that manages a registry of HDAs. For example, the Federal Aviation Authority or the Japan Civil Aviation Bureau could be RAAs. The RAA is a 14-bit field, giving 16,384 RAAs. An RAA MUST provide a set of services to allocate HDAs to organizations, and SHOULD have a public policy on what is necessary to obtain an HDA. The RAA need not maintain any HIP-related services; at minimum it MUST maintain a DNS zone for the HDA zone delegation used to discover the HIP Rendezvous Servers for the HID.

The two levels of hierarchy allow civil aviation authorities to have at least one RAA for their national air space. Within its RAAs, the authorities can delegate HDAs as needed, and there may be other RAAs allowed to operate within a given air space, which is a policy decision of each authority.

The HDA is the entity that actually issues identifiers. It maintains a registry of DETs, and it is the one that can endorse a device's registration. Because DETs under administrative control may be used in many different domains such as commercial, recreation and military, RAAs should be careful about the HDA structure they hand out.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two levels on purpose. The top level is a national or regional authority, such as a civil aviation regulator. It hands out blocks of the address space to organisations below it, and those organisations issue the actual drone identifiers. The RFC gives each level 14 bits, so there are 16,384 authorities at each level.

sections.title: Building the ORCHID
sections.content:
The section improves on ORCHIDv2 with three enhancements: the inclusion of an optional Info field between the Prefix and the ORCHID Generation Algorithm ID, an increase in flexibility on the length of each component in the ORCHID construction provided the resulting ORCHID is 128 bits, and the use of cSHAKE for the hashing function. The cSHAKE extendable output function is based on Keccak and is a variable output length hash function, so it does not use the truncation operation other hashes need; the invocation specifies the desired number of bits in the hash output. cSHAKE also has a customization string parameter, which is used for including the ORCHID Context Identifier in a standard fashion.

The new construction is ORCHID := Prefix (p) | Info (n) | OGA ID (o) | Hash (m), where the prefix is an IPv6 prefix of at most 28 bits, the Info field is n bits that define a use of the ORCHID and may be zero, the OGA ID is a 4- or 8-bit identifier for the hash function in use, which for HHIT generation is the HHIT Suite ID, and the hash is m bits long. The lengths must sum to 128 bits. For HHITs with a 28-bit IPv6 prefix, 100 bits remain to be divided between the Info field, the OGA ID and the hash output; the hash portion is 64 bits here, which the RFC says may be as small as is acceptable, and the Info field, the HID, takes the remaining 28 bits.

The input to the hash function explicitly includes all the header content plus the Context ID, and the header content consists of the prefix, the Info field and the OGA ID. The length of the resulting hash is set by the sum of the length of the ORCHID header fields, so a 28-bit prefix with 28 bits for the HID and 8 bits for the OGA ID leaves 64 bits for the hash length. The cSHAKE function call is cSHAKE128(Input, L, '', Context ID), where the input is the prefix, the additional information, the OGA ID and the HOST_ID, and L is the length in bits of the hash portion of the ORCHID. The Context ID for the HHIT hash is a fixed value, 0x00B5 A69C 795D F5D5 F008 7F56 843F 2C40, and context IDs are allocated out of the namespace introduced for Cryptographically Generated Addresses type tags.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash is computed over the whole header, not just the key, so nobody can substitute one part of the address for another. The hash function is cSHAKE128, which can be told to produce exactly as many bits as are needed instead of a fixed length that then has to be trimmed.

sections.title: Proving Ownership of a DET
sections.content:
DETs are registered to HDAs. The registration process defined in the DRIP registration specification ensures DET global uniqueness, and it also allows the mechanism to create UAS public and private data that are associated with the DET.

The EdDSA25519 host identity underlying the DET can be used in an 88-byte self-proof evidence, consisting of timestamps, the HHIT and a signature over them, to provide proof to observers of Remote ID ownership. In practice, the Wrapper and Manifest authentication formats implicitly provide this self-proof evidence. A lookup service like DNS can provide the host identity and registration proof.

For observers without Internet access, a 200-byte offline self-endorsement could provide the same Remote ID ownership proof. The endorsement contains the HDA's signing of the UA's HHIT, itself signed by the UA's host identity. Only a small cache containing the HDA's host identity, HHIT and metadata is needed by the observer. However, such an object would just fit in the ASTM Authentication Message with no room for growth. In practice, the DRIP authentication specification provides this offline self-endorsement in two authentication messages: the HDA's endorsement of the UA's HHIT registration in a Link authentication message whose hash is sent in a Manifest authentication message.

Hashes of any previously sent ASTM messages can be placed in a Manifest authentication message. When a Location/Vector Message, which provides the UA's location, altitude, heading, speed and status, is hashed along with the hash of the HDA's UA HHIT endorsement and sent in a Manifest authentication message, an observer who can also see the UA at the claimed location has very strong proof of the UA's Remote ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier alone proves nothing. The proof comes from the drone signing the identifier with its private key, and from the organisation that issued the identifier signing it too. An observer that can check both, and can see the drone at the position it claims, has good grounds to trust the link between the identifier and the aircraft.

sections.title: Finding a DET in DNS
sections.content:
There are two approaches for storing and retrieving DETs using DNS, given as examples to guide deployment. The document does not recommend which approach to use, and further DNS-related considerations are covered in the DRIP registration specification.

The first approach is as fully qualified domain names, for example 20010030.hhit.arpa.. The second is reverse DNS lookups as IPv6 addresses. A DET can be used to construct an FQDN that points to the service that has the public and private information for the UA. Assuming the RAA is decimal 100 and the HDA is decimal 50, the PTR record is constructed as 100.50.20010030.hhit.arpa. IN PTR foo.uss.example.org., and the HDA SHOULD provide DNS service for its zone and provide the HHIT detail response.

The DET reverse lookup can be a standard IPv6 reverse lookup, or it can leverage the HHIT structure. Using the allocated prefix 2001:30::/28, with the RAA decimal 10 and the HDA decimal 20, the DET is 2001:30:280:1405:a3ad:1952:ad0:a69e. A reverse lookup could be written as a69e.0ad0.1952.a3ad.1405.0280.20.10.20010030.hhit.arpa., or in a more compact form a3ad19520ad0a69e.5.20.10.20010030.hhit.arpa.. A standard ip6.arpa record has the advantage that only one registry service is supported. The DNS entry for the DET can also provide a revocation service: instead of returning the host identity record it may return a record showing that the host identity, and thus the DET, has been revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier can be looked up in DNS either forwards or backwards, because the address encodes which registry issued it. The same lookup can return a revocation marker instead of the record, so a withdrawn identifier stops resolving to a valid owner.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The 64-bit hash in HHITs presents a real risk of a second-preimage cryptographic hash attack, and there are no known studies of hash size impact on such attacks. With today's computing power, producing 2^64 EdDSA keypairs and then generating the corresponding HHIT is economically feasible. A single bitcoin mining ASIC can do on the order of 2^46 SHA-256 hashes per second, or about 2^62 hashes in a single day, so 2^64 is not prohibitive, especially as it can be done in parallel.

That figure is for stealing a specific HHIT. Consider a street photography company with 1,024 UAs, each with its own HHIT; an attacker may well be satisfied stealing any one of them, and then only needs to satisfy what is equivalent to a 54-bit condition. So although the probability of a collision or pre-image attack is low in a collection of 1,024 HHITs out of a total population of 2^64, it is computationally and economically feasible. Therefore the HHIT registration is a MUST, and registration validation SHOULD be performed by observers either through registry lookups or via broadcast registration proofs.

The DET registry services effectively block attempts to take over or hijack a DET, but they do not stop a rogue attempting to impersonate a known DET. That attack can be mitigated by the receiver of messages containing DETs using DNS to find the host identity for the DET, so the use of DNSSEC by the DET registries is recommended to provide trust in host identity retrieval. Another mitigation of HHIT hijacking is when the host identity owner supplies an object containing the HHIT that is signed by the host identity private key of the HDA.

The two risks with HHITs are the use of an invalid HID and forced HIT collisions. The use of a DNS zone is strong protection against invalid HIDs, querying an HDA's Rendezvous Server for a HIT under the HDA protects against talking to unregistered clients, and the registry service, through its HHIT uniqueness enforcement, provides protection against forced or accidental hash collisions.

Post-quantum computing is out of scope. UAs and broadcast Remote ID communications are so constrained that current post-quantum cryptography is not applicable, and because a UA may use a unique DET for each operation the attack window could be limited to the duration of the operation. HHITs contain the identifier for the cryptographic suite used in their creation, so a future algorithm that is safe for post-quantum computing and fits the Remote ID constraints may readily be added.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash is only 64 bits, and that is small enough that a determined attacker could search for a collision on purpose. That is why registering the identifier is not optional: the registry is what stops two devices ending up with the same one.

items.text: Out of scope, but the suite identifier is in the tag, so a new algorithm can be added.
